nodes.name: Anterior (flexor-pronator) compartment
nodes.location: Palm side of the forearm, in a surface, a middle and a deep layer from the elbow to the wrist.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends the wrist and the fingers and turns the palm down.
nodes.shapeNote: Together these muscles make up most of the palm-side fullness of the forearm. Which muscle shapes which part of that outline cannot be read from the surface. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for the individual muscles inside it.
nodes.name: Posterior (extensor-supinator) compartment
nodes.location: Back of the forearm and its thumb-side edge, in a surface layer and a deep layer from the elbow to the wrist.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens the wrist, the fingers and the thumb and turns the palm up. The brachioradialis, also in this group, bends the elbow.
nodes.shapeNote: Makes up the back of the forearm and, through the brachioradialis and the thumb-side wrist extensors, the thumb-side outline near the elbow. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

caveats: Studies disagree on whether turning the palm up, sideways or down changes how hard it works in a curl.
From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up; that is not counted as a separate action here.
nodes.name: Brachioradialis
nodes.location: Thumb side of the forearm, from just above the elbow to the wrist; the outermost muscle on that edge.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your elbow. It works whichever way the palm faces; anatomy texts describe it as strongest with the thumb pointing up.
nodes.shapeNote: Contributes to the thumb-side contour of the upper forearm, the bulge just below the elbow. It does not bend the wrist. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

caveats: Its tendon is easy to see at the wrist; a visible tendon is not muscle size.
nodes.name: Flexor carpi radialis
nodes.location: Palm side, surface layer, running at a slant from the pinky side of the elbow to the thumb side of the wrist.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your wrist toward the palm and toward the thumb side.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the palm-side contour toward the thumb side, between the elbow crease and mid-forearm. It is not the whole thumb-side width: the brachioradialis forms that edge. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

nodes.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
nodes.location: Palm side, surface layer, along the pinky-side edge from the elbow to the wrist.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your wrist toward the palm and toward the pinky side.
nodes.shapeNote: Contributes to the palm-side contour along the pinky side (ulnar). Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

caveats: Absent on one or both sides in some people; how often varies widely between populations.
Its absence has not been shown to reduce grip strength.
nodes.name: Palmaris longus
nodes.location: Palm side, surface layer, down the middle: a short belly near the elbow and a long tendon to the palm.
nodes.whatItDoes: Tenses the sheet of connective tissue in the palm and gives a little help bending the wrist.
nodes.shapeNote: Small belly and long tendon, and missing in some people, so it is not a major driver of forearm width. Visible shape depends far more on the muscles around it.

caveats: Grip and finger-curl work loads it together with the deep finger flexor (FDP); how the work splits between them is not known.
nodes.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis
nodes.location: Palm side, middle layer: under the surface wrist flexors and over the deep finger flexor.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your four fingers at their middle joints, and helps bend the knuckles and the wrist. Each finger has its own part of the muscle, but the parts do not work fully apart.
nodes.shapeNote: May add to the general fullness of the palm side of the forearm. It lies under other muscles, so it has no separately visible outline.

caveats: Grip and finger-curl work loads it together with FDS; how the work splits between them is not known.
nodes.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
nodes.location: Palm side, deep layer, against the ulna on the pinky side and under the other finger flexors.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your fingertips: it is the only muscle that bends the end joints of the four fingers. It also helps bend the middle joints, the knuckles and the wrist.
nodes.shapeNote: Deep bulk under the palm-side muscles. It may add to overall palm-side thickness but has little or no separately visible surface contour, so it is not drawn as a surface stripe.

caveats: Hard to feel through the skin because it lies under the other flexors.
nodes.name: Flexor pollicis longus
nodes.location: Palm side, deep layer, on the thumb side against the radius.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends the tip of your thumb, and helps bend the thumb at its knuckle. No other muscle bends the thumb tip.
nodes.shapeNote: Deep tissue on the thumb side of the palm side, close to the bone; little or no separately visible contour.

caveats: Both pronators turn the palm down, so palm-down work loads it together with the pronator quadratus.
nodes.name: Pronator teres
nodes.location: Palm side just below the elbow, surface layer, slanting from the pinky side of the elbow to the middle of the radius on the thumb side.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your palm down, and gives a little help bending the elbow.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the slanted palm-side contour just below the elbow crease, where it forms the pinky-side edge of the hollow in front of the elbow. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

caveats: Both pronators turn the palm down, so palm-down work loads it together with the pronator teres.
nodes.name: Pronator quadratus
nodes.location: Palm side, deepest layer: a flat, square muscle on the two forearm bones just above the wrist.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your palm down, and helps hold the two forearm bones together near the wrist.
nodes.shapeNote: Deep and close to the bones near the wrist, under the flexor tendons; little or no direct surface definition.

caveats: Ordinary exercises cannot train it apart from ECRB; the two are counted together in practice.
nodes.name: Extensor carpi radialis longus
nodes.location: Back of the forearm on the thumb side, starting just above the elbow beside the brachioradialis.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your wrist back and toward the thumb side.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the contour on the back and thumb side of the forearm near the elbow. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

caveats: Ordinary exercises cannot train it apart from ECRL; the two are counted together in practice.
In one study it was more active in wrist-extension holds with the palm turned down. That is short-term muscle activity, not growth.
nodes.name: Extensor carpi radialis brevis
nodes.location: Back of the forearm on the thumb side, beside and partly under ECRL.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your wrist back and toward the thumb side.
nodes.shapeNote: Part of the extensor mass on the back and thumb side of the forearm. Partly covered by ECRL, so its own outline is only partly visible. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

nodes.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
nodes.location: Back of the forearm, surface layer, along the pinky-side edge from the elbow to the wrist.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your wrist back and toward the pinky side.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the contour along the back of the forearm on the pinky side. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

nodes.name: Extensor digitorum
nodes.location: Back of the forearm, surface layer, down the middle; it splits into four tendons that run to the fingers.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your four fingers, mainly at the knuckles, and helps bend the wrist back.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the central mass on the back of the forearm. Its tendons on the back of the hand are tendon, not muscle bulk. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

caveats: Some anatomists treat it as the pinky-side part of the extensor digitorum.
nodes.name: Extensor digiti minimi
nodes.location: Back of the forearm, surface layer: a thin muscle on the pinky side of the extensor digitorum.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your little finger, on its own or with the other fingers.
nodes.shapeNote: Small, and joined to the extensor digitorum near the elbow; not a major independent driver of forearm width.

nodes.name: Extensor indicis
nodes.location: Back of the forearm, deep layer near the wrist, arising on the pinky side; its tendon runs to the index finger.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your index finger, which lets it point on its own.
nodes.shapeNote: Small and deep near the wrist; little or no separately visible contour.

caveats: References disagree about a small effect at the wrist, so no wrist action is counted for it here.
nodes.name: Abductor pollicis longus
nodes.location: Back of the forearm, deep layer, coming to the surface on the thumb side above the wrist on its way to the base of the thumb.
nodes.whatItDoes: Moves your thumb out from the hand at its base, away from the index finger, and helps straighten it there.
nodes.shapeNote: Mostly deep, with little separately visible contour. Near the wrist its tendon, with EPB's, forms the thumb-side edge of the hollow at the base of the thumb; a visible tendon there is not muscle size.

caveats: Where its tendon attaches varies a good deal between people.
nodes.name: Extensor pollicis brevis
nodes.location: Back of the forearm, deep layer near the wrist on the thumb side, beside APL.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your thumb at its knuckle, and helps straighten it at its base.
nodes.shapeNote: Small and deep, with little separately visible contour. Its tendon at the base of the thumb can be easy to see; that is tendon, not muscle size.

nodes.name: Extensor pollicis longus
nodes.location: Back of the forearm, deep layer in the middle; a long tendon bends around a bony bump on the back of the radius to reach the thumb tip.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens the tip of your thumb, and helps straighten the thumb at its knuckle.
nodes.shapeNote: Deep muscle with little or no separately visible contour. Its long tendon forms the pinky-side edge of the hollow at the base of the thumb; a visible tendon is not muscle size.

caveats: With the elbow bent the biceps is the stronger palm-up muscle, so palm-up work with a bent elbow is not supinator-only.
nodes.name: Supinator
nodes.location: Just below the elbow on the back and thumb side, deep layer, wrapped around the top of the radius.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your palm up.
nodes.shapeNote: Deep near the elbow, under the surface extensors; not directly visible in an ordinary surface view.

caveats: Shown beside the forearm muscles because of where it sits; forearm specialization does not target it.
nodes.name: Anconeus
nodes.location: Back of the elbow: a small triangle from the thumb-side bony knob of the upper-arm bone to the point of the elbow.
nodes.whatItDoes: Helps straighten your elbow and steadies the joint; the triceps does most of the straightening.
nodes.shapeNote: Small; may add to the contour at the back of the elbow. It is not a forearm growth target.

nodes.name: Biceps brachii
nodes.location: Front of the upper arm, crossing the elbow to the radius.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your elbow and turns your palm up; with the elbow bent it is the strongest palm-up muscle.
nodes.shapeNote: Shapes the front of the upper arm. It is an upper-arm muscle and does not add forearm size.
caveats: Shown only as another muscle that curls and palm-up turning load; not a forearm target.

nodes.name: Brachialis
nodes.location: Front of the lower upper arm, under the biceps, crossing the elbow to the ulna.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your elbow, whichever way the palm faces. It does not turn the forearm.
nodes.shapeNote: Mostly covered by the biceps; may show at the sides of the lower upper arm. It is not a forearm muscle.
caveats: Shown only as another muscle that curls load; not a forearm target.

sources.notes: Checked via web-search results (abstract): standard EMG texts held that ECRL and ECRB activity cannot be distinguished even with intramuscular electrodes; the authors placed fine-wire electrodes from cadaver measurements (10 specimens) and reported differentiated recordings in three volunteers. A methods paper, not a training study.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Extensor Carpi Ulnaris Muscle (Sawyer, Sajjad, Tadi)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: posterior forearm muscle that primarily extends and adducts the wrist, with ECRL and ECRB for extension and with FCU for adduction; humeral and ulnar heads; inserts on the dorsal base of the fifth metacarpal via the sixth extensor compartment; posterior interosseous nerve.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: extensor digitorum
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: extends the proximal phalanges at the MCP joints and the fingers at the interphalangeal joints; assists extension of the hand at the wrist.

sources.title: Kenhub: extensor digitorum muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: also participates in wrist extension; its belly ends in four tendons about a third of the way down the forearm, passing under the extensor retinaculum to digits 2–5.

sources.title: StatPearls: wrist and finger extensor muscles (NBK534805)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: extensor digitorum communis extends the index, middle, ring and little fingers; extensor indicis proprius independently extends the index finger; extensor digiti minimi independently extends the little finger. The article's exact title was not shown in the results (another site cites it as Wrist Extensor Muscles).

sources.title: Kenhub: extensor digiti minimi muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: long, thin muscle of the superficial extensor group; proximal fibres usually fused with extensor digitorum, separate from about mid-forearm, just medial to it; extends the fifth digit at the MCP joint; posterior interosseous nerve.

sources.title: University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences: muscles of the upper limb
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: extensor digiti minimi inserts into the extensor expansion of the fifth digit, and some anatomists regard it as the ulnar-most part of extensor digitorum; extensor indicis arises from the distal posterior ulna and interosseous membrane, joins the index tendon of extensor digitorum and extends the index finger.

sources.title: Kenhub: extensor indicis muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: narrow, elongated deep extensor of the posterior compartment; extends the index finger at the MCP and interphalangeal joints, letting it extend on its own; weaker wrist-extension effect; posterior interosseous nerve.

sources.title: Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center El Paso: muscles of the upper limb, listed alphabetically
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results (only some rows were shown): abductor pollicis longus abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint; the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis form the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox; anconeus runs from the lateral epicondyle to the olecranon and upper ulna and extends the forearm.

sources.title: Kenhub: abductor pollicis longus muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint; the English article also lists extension of the hand at the wrist, while the German article and video describe radial deviation.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: abductor pollicis longus
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: abducts and extends the thumb at the first carpometacarpal joint; no wrist action listed.

sources.title: Kenhub: extensor pollicis brevis muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: small, deep forearm muscle; extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal and MCP joints; with the abductor pollicis longus tendon forms the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox; posterior interosseous nerve.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: extensor pollicis brevis
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: extends the proximal phalanx of the thumb at the first MCP joint and the first metacarpal at the first carpometacarpal joint; inserts on the dorsal base of the proximal phalanx.

sources.title: Jabir et al., The Extensor Pollicis Brevis: A Review of Its Anatomy and Variations (Eplasty)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: textbook descriptions of the EPB tendon disagree with published anatomical studies; in one cadaver study only a quarter of tendons inserted in the conventional way, into the base of the proximal phalanx.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Extensor Pollicis Longus Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: thumb extensor at the MCP and IP joints (with some adduction); arises from the middle third of the posterior ulna, passes over Lister's tubercle and is the only occupant of the third extensor compartment; its tendon is the ulnar boundary of the anatomical snuffbox; posterior interosseous nerve. Updated 21 Dec 2022.

sources.title: Kenhub: extensor pollicis longus muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: main action is thumb extension at the MCP and interphalangeal joints, with a weak contribution to wrist extension.

sources.title: Kenhub: supinator muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: spiral muscle of the deep part of the posterior compartment that wraps around the proximal radius and rotates it laterally (supination); found deep in the forearm, superficial only to the radius and ulna; posterior interosseous nerve.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: supinator
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: supinates the forearm at the radioulnar joints; tested against resistance with the elbow extended, which keeps biceps brachii from contributing to supination.

sources.title: Kenhub: anconeus muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: small triangular muscle at the back of the elbow from the lateral epicondyle to the lateral olecranon; helps extend the forearm at the elbow and helps stabilise the joint; some authors consider it a continuation of triceps; radial nerve.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: anconeus
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: posterior and superficial to the elbow joint; extends the forearm at the elbow joint.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Biceps Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results (introduction): a forearm flexor when the elbow is extended that becomes the forearm's most powerful supinator when the elbow is flexed; inserts on the radial tuberosity; musculocutaneous nerve.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Brachialis Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results (introduction): flexes the elbow in all physiological positions and is considered a pure flexor; no supination or pronation; lies in the anteroinferior arm, deeper than the biceps; inserts on the ulnar tuberosity.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Muscles
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results (introduction and structure): an anterior (flexor) and a posterior (extensor) compartment holding about twenty muscles, each subdivided into superficial and deep parts. Updated 5 Jun 2023.

sources.title: Kenhub: superficial anterior forearm muscles
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: groups pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis as superficial anterior muscles sharing the common flexor origin on the medial epicondyle (a teaching source places FDS in a middle layer beneath the first four).

sources.title: Kenhub: superficial extensors of the forearm
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: brachioradialis, ECRL, ECRB, extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi and ECU form the superficial posterior group, mostly from the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle; anconeus is discussed with the arm muscles.

sources.title: Kenhub: deep extensors of the forearm
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results: the deep posterior group acts on the thumb and index finger, except the supinator, which acts on the proximal radioulnar joint. The group's members (supinator, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis longus and brevis, extensor indicis) were listed in Kenhub's extensor indicis article (A37) rather than on this page's visible excerpt.

sources.title: Kleiber, Kunz and Disselhorst-Klug, Muscular coordination of biceps brachii and brachioradialis in elbow flexion with respect to hand position (Frontiers in Physiology, 2015)
sources.notes: 16 healthy adults, slow single elbow flexions (20 degrees per second) with the hand pronated, neutral and supinated; surface EMG. The brachioradialis's contribution differed in pronation from supination and neutral, while biceps activity did not change with hand position; the authors relate this to the biceps's mechanical disadvantage in pronation. Acute, light task; other EMG studies disagree on the size of the position effect.

sources.title: Mogk and Keir, The effects of posture on forearm muscle loading during gripping (Ergonomics 46(9):956-975, 2003)
sources.notes: 10 adults gripping a dynamometer at several efforts in three wrist and three forearm postures. Wrist-extensor activity accompanied gripping, was generally larger than flexor activity at low to moderate grip forces, and was always greater with the forearm pronated. Supports the wrist extensors steadying the wrist whenever the hand grips; a dynamometer is not a barbell, and EMG is not a growth measure.

sources.title: Jukic et al. (2021), lifting straps in the deadlift: movement velocity, grip strength and perceived grip security (Physiology & Behavior 229:113283)
sources.notes: 16 men deadlifting 4 sets of 4 with and without straps. With straps, grip strength fell less across the session and recovered faster, and grip felt more secure. Supports treating a strapped set's grip demand as different from an unstrapped one; it does not measure forearm muscle activity.

sources.title: Goetz et al., contribution of the flexor pollicis longus to pinch strength, measured before and after an EMG-guided lidocaine block (2012; PubMed 23101527)
sources.notes: 11 healthy volunteers; key, three-point and tip pinch strength fell after the flexor pollicis longus was temporarily blocked. Supports the long thumb flexor working in pinches; pinch-meter tasks, not plate pinches, and only the abstract was read.

sources.title: Kondi et al., An electromyographic study comparing muscle function during supination and pronation of the forearm (Cureus, 2026)
sources.notes: Pilot study, 4 adults, forearm held in neutral against a 1 kg load at increasing distances from the rotation axis (a lever). In supination the supinator was more active than the biceps at low torque and the biceps rose more steeply as torque increased; in pronation the pronator quadratus was more active at low torque and the pronator teres rose more steeply. Surface EMG for the pronators, fine wire for the supinator; isometric; very small sample.

sources.title: O'Sullivan and Gallwey, Upper-limb surface electro-myography at maximum supination and pronation torques: the effect of elbow and forearm angle (Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology 12(4):275-285, 2002)
sources.notes: 24 men, maximal pronation and supination efforts at four elbow angles and three forearm angles, surface EMG of six muscles including pronator teres, biceps and brachioradialis. Torque in both directions changed with elbow and forearm angle. Supports recording the elbow angle on the lever rows; maximal isometric efforts, not repetitions.

sources.title: Pratt, Hoffman, Grainger and Ditroilo, Forearm electromyographic activity during the deadlift exercise is affected by grip type and sex (Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology, 2020)
sources.notes: Trained lifters deadlifting at 50, 70 and 90 per cent of their maximum with hook, mixed and double-overhand grips; forearm EMG changed with grip type and load. Cited only for that: secondary summaries disagree on which grip ranked highest, and the full text was not read.

sources.title: Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center El Paso: axilla, posterior shoulder and arm muscle tables
sources.notes: The arm companion to S4, for the two upper-arm muscles the forearm atlas credits as external contributors: biceps brachii (elbow flexion, supination) and brachialis (elbow flexion only). Actions, not exercise loading.

mappingVersion.methodNotes: Each catalog exercise the forearm atlas maps has one default variant (cat-<id>) with its execution spelled out: organization, forearm orientation, wrist position, grip, straps, laterality, measure, deliberate hold, and an elbow angle only where the exercise defines one. Each mapping names one muscle, one joint action, a relationship (direct, contributing, stabilizer, incidental) and a muscle mode (dynamic or isometric) separately, so one set can be dynamic elbow flexion and isometric wrist stabilization at once. Mappings are by catalog id; no name matching. A mapping is reviewed when the muscle's action is sourced (anatomy tables S4, S7, S8, the arm reference M8) and the relationship is explained in its rationale; EMG sources (S2, S3, M1, M2, M5-M7) are cited only for what they measured. Everything else stays draft and is shown as pending review, never counted. FDS and FDP are always credited together as shared: nothing in an ordinary grip separates them. Grip during rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, deadlifts, shrugs and hangs is incidental and is not earned by a set logged with straps. No percentage splits between muscles, no mapping credits every forearm muscle, the hand's own muscles are not credited to the forearm, and a broad 'forearms' tag on an unmapped exercise stays region-level.
